title: Connect two people across apps
summary: One person shows a code or sends a link that names a per-encounter messaging identifier with its relays and a fresh single-use handle; the other scans it, proposes the relationship, and both issue a relationship credential to each other. Two existing registry tasks, no third party. Every step carries a proof. When both are offline the proposal is shown back as a code and the rest follows once a carrier exists.

inviter.description: Shows the code or sends the link that names its per-encounter messaging identifier, relays and challenge; accepts the proposal and issues a credential about the responder.

responder.description: Scans the code or opens the link; proposes the relationship and issues a credential about the inviter.

propose.description: The responder's proposal and the inviter's acceptance (its #response, naming the inviter's pairwise relationship identifier). The proposal's id is the responder's fresh challenge and the threadId of every later document; ceremony.enactment is the handle from the inviter's link, minted by the inviter alone and single-use: the inviter accepts one proposal per handle and refuses every later one, so one link connects one person. The proposal is sent to a relay named in the inviter's identifier, or shown back as a code when both are offline; an inviter accepts a first message from an identifier it has never seen only while its handle is live. Every document of this and the following steps, request and response alike, carries a proof with the recipient in band, signed by the authentication key of the issuer's messaging identifier; issuer, proof signer and transport sender are one identifier (propose 0.1 makes the proof optional, this ceremony does not).

issue-inviter.description: The inviter's relationship credential about the responder, and the responder's receipt (its #response, carrying the digest of the credential as stored). Follows the acceptance and may travel with it. The credential is signed by the inviter's pairwise relationship identifier, which is not its messaging identifier.

issue-responder.description: The responder's relationship credential about the inviter, and the inviter's receipt. Follows the acceptance and does not wait for the inviter's credential; the two issue steps may cross. Signed by the responder's pairwise relationship identifier.

sideEffects.rationale: Each party mints a credential about the other. Not compensatable by this ceremony; revocation is the issuer's own act.

exposure.rationale: Each issue step delivers credential material the other party retains, and each party issues on its own authority about a person present or named. enactmentPrivacy is shared because the two parties are meant to know they share this flow, and the pairwise relationship identifiers already correlate the pair. A leaked pair of credentials names the two relationship identifiers, the handle and the two challenges: it links everything else issued under those relationship identifiers, and nothing beyond them as long as each identifier is made for this one relationship and appears in no other disclosure; the messaging identifiers are per encounter and add no further link. Evidence is countersigned in the bilateral sense of mutual-attestation/0.1: both parties sign steps of the one enactment; no step carries prev digests of another.

org.real-life.rltp.note: The definition proposed in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1034 (three steps, 8 November 2026), kept here so DTGWG tooling and the test vector agree on one text. The flow is implemented in lib/src/shared-connect.ts and exercised by vectors/shared-connect.json. Until the registry publishes the definition, steps carry {enactment, step} (and terminal: true on the last step) and no definition or definitionDigest.
org.real-life.rltp.entry: A VTI trigger link on the shared origin: https://link.trustoverip.org/t#_from=<per-encounter peer DID>&_id=<16-byte challenge, canonical base64url>&_exp=<epoch seconds>&_type=/vti/flow/shared-connect/0.1[&_label=<display name, code shown in person only>]. _from is a did:peer:2 or a long-form did:peer:4 naming each relay of the inviter as a service, or none where the inviter names no relay (the link is valid either way); _id is ceremony.enactment. A code shown in person expires within 10 minutes, a link sent in a message within 7 days.
org.real-life.rltp.identifiers: Two layers on each side: a per-encounter messaging identifier (the inviter's is the peer DID in _from, the responder's is the propose issuer) and a pairwise relationship identifier (relationshipDid: an Ed25519 did:key or did:peer:0, made for this one relationship; it signs the credential and stays stable while the messaging identifier may change). What an observer sees depends on the carrier: a relay carrying sealed documents sees the messaging identifiers and the timing, not the relationship identifiers or the content; anyone who sees a code sees what it carries, the inviter's messaging identifier and handle in the link, and in the offline back-code also the responder's messaging identifier, its relationship identifier (rel), its name (n) and the proof; a code that carries a card shows its side's relationship identifier, and the pair's key agreement key as well, which is why a card travels only in a code shown in person.
org.real-life.rltp.credential: Each issue carries a VC of types VerifiableCredential, DTGCredential and RelationshipCredential under the two registry contexts only (credentials/v2 and the DTG context), issuerScope pairwise. It cites the enactment with the DTG spec's own members (Trust Task Context Binding): taskContext is the id of the propose, the document that opened the exchange (also the responder's challenge), and taskDigestMultibase its task digest (JCS without the proof, sha-256, base58btc). Both credentials of one enactment cite the same propose, so a third party pairs them without the transport; the propose is their outcome evidence. credentialSubject carries {id: the other party's relationshipDid} and the issuer's own observation of the channel as the IRI https://real-life.org/rltp/v1#channel (scan | displayed | link | sent), the one member DTG has no term for yet (proposed to dtgwg-cred-spec). No vendor context, no EncounterCredential type: a wallet stores the credential without bundling anything of RLTP's (Keyring, 8 November 2026).
org.real-life.rltp.offline: When neither side has a network the responder shows its signed proposal back as a code in a reconstruction form (_from=<responder's peer DID>, _id=<the proposal's id, the responder's challenge>, _type=/vti/flow/shared-connect/0.1/back, rel=<relationshipDid>, t=<issuedAt as epoch seconds>, n=<reason, percent-encoded>, sig=<proofValue>); the inviter rebuilds the propose document, with ceremony.enactment taken from the handle it issued and holds locally, and verifies the proof. The form requires: no expiresAt, issuedAt in whole seconds, proof.created equal to issuedAt, and the verification method being the authentication method of _from. Measured 466 to 584 characters. The acceptance and the issue steps then follow over any carrier, at any later time. A code shown in person may also carry its side's card, the card of the issue step without its delivery hints (the pair's X25519 key under a proof of the pairwise relationship identifier, with a challenge), in reconstruction form under names without the reserved underscore, which a reader that does not know them passes over: the link the inviter's (rel=<relationshipDid>, t=<the card's challenge.issuedAt and proof.created as epoch seconds>, ka=<keyAgreement>, csig=<the card's proofValue>; the card's challenge is the first 16 bytes, base64url, of sha-256 over the JCS of {ceremony: <this ceremony's URI>, exp: <_exp as a number>, from: <_from>, id: <_id>}, so the pairwise identifier states which messaging identifier, handle and expiry it stands behind; each of the four names occurs once), the back-code the responder's (ka, csig beside its rel and t; the card's challenge is the same digest over {ceremony, enactment: <the inviter's handle>, from: <the back-code's _from>, id: <the proposal's id>}, its time the proposal's issuedAt). A reader that knows the names rebuilds the card and verifies it, and refuses a code whose card does not verify. With both cards each side holds the other's pairwise keys after the two codes, without a carrier: an RLTP responder treats the relationship as there when it shows the back-code, an RLTP inviter when its person accepts a proposal read from one. Once the inviter's acceptance has arrived the responder shows no back-code: an RLTP responder that read a card in the link takes the relationship from the card in the inviter's issue step, or from the card in the link where that issue carries none. The acceptance must name the relationshipDid of the card in the link, and a card in an issue step the same key as the card in the code. A card adds about 225 characters to a code (651 for the link and 663 for the back-code of the vector); a producer leaves the card out of a link that would pass 990 characters, and writes no card into a link sent in a message; a back-code with a card that would pass 1200 characters (a long name in the proposal) is not shown, and nothing opens from it. The delivery hints of a side travel in the card of its issue step, by a carrier: until then nothing is delivered on the relationship. Who shows a code decides what it says: a code shown on from another person's screen connects to that person, as with any code.
org.real-life.rltp.freshness: The proposal is accepted before the link's _exp, with 60 seconds of clock tolerance in the document's favour; it has no age limit of its own, so a link sent in a message is answered while the inviter is offline and the proposal is taken when the inviter fetches it. A code shown in person expires within 10 minutes, which bounds the age of its proposal as well. A document whose issuedAt lies in the future is refused. The acceptance, the issue steps and the receipts have no window of their own: each answers in the thread of a document this side holds, so their timestamps are read as evidence, not as commands, and an inbox fetched late or an inviter that was offline when the proposal arrived still completes. No maxDuration is declared for this reason.
org.real-life.rltp.proofs: Step proofs are eddsa-jcs-2022 by an Ed25519 key under authentication of the messaging identifier (#key-1 as this library writes its DIDs; a did:peer:0 relationship identifier names its one method <did>#<multikey>); credential proofs by the relationship identifier under assertionMethod, with the credential's @context repeated in the proof.
